title: Драка в зале и мёртвые рыбки  (Brawl in the Dining Room and the Dead Fish)

segments.t: To Vasily's amusement, a full-blown brawl breaks out in the dining room, prompting Vika to strip Senya of his monthly bonus. Worse still, Sasha and Kostya horrifiedly discover that Max killed the aquarium fish Ilya had gifted her, and Kostya tells Max to leave.
Что ты с салатами в зале жонглировал?
Значит, в этом месяце работаешь без премии.
Костян, я должен был ему отомстить.
Let's replay the exchange and look closely at each Russian phrase.
'Although what kind of restaurant is this, anyway?' Max prompts decisively to Kostya here, linking "restoran" ("restaurant"), "khotya" ("at least"), and "kakoy" ("what a, how") in one brisk exchange.
'Naked men running through the dining room.' Vika holds a candid direction in this beat, using "golyye" (from "golyy", "bare, naked") alongside "muzhiki" ("lads, guys") to shape the meaning.
Что ты с салатами в зале жонглировал?
'Why were you juggling salads out in the dining room?' Kostya tests promptly to Max here, leaning on "salatami" ("salad") before closing the thought with "zale" ("hall").
'You red-headed clown.' Max projects a warm style as they talk, leaning on "kloun" ("clown") before closing the thought with "ryzhiy" ("red-haired").
Значит, в этом месяце работаешь без премии.
'That means you are working without a bonus this month.' Vika maintains a resolute angle in front of Kostya, leaning on "znachit" ("then, so") before closing the thought with "mesyatse" ("month").
'Did everyone hear that?' Kostya probes decisively without hesitation, putting "slyshali" ("did you hear") alongside "vse" ("all") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Right, Vika?' Max tests calmly for Kostya's benefit, pairing "da" ("yes") with "vika" ("Vika") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
'My guests are going to walk out.' Vika holds a playful stance for Max, pairing "pokinut" ("to leave, to vacate") with "mne" ("to me") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
'What a madhouse.' Kostya conveys a lively stance straight away, anchoring the Russian line on "dome" ("house") and "kakoy" ("what a, how") without extra filler.
Костян, я должен был ему отомстить.
'Kostyan, I had to get back at him.' Max strikes a brisk rhythm across the room, combining "dolzhen" ("has to, must") and "byl" ("was") so the key meaning lands right away.
'Oh, stop whining.' Vika brings an honest manner without hesitation, leaning on "noy" ("to whine, to complain") before closing the thought with "nu" ("oh, come on").
'Did you kill them?' Kostya asks dryly as the beat lands, weaving "ubil" ("killed") together with "eto" ("this") just the way native speakers do.
'Max, you had better leave.' Vika picks an honest stance straight away, anchoring the Russian line on "luchshe" ("better") and "uyti" ("to leave") without extra filler.
Что ты с салатами в зале жонглировал?
Значит, в этом месяце работаешь без премии.
Костян, я должен был ему отомстить.
That wraps up this scene as a wild brawl erupts in the dining room to Vasily's delight, while Sasha and Kostya discover that Max poisoned the aquarium fish Ilya gave to Sasha. Until next time!
